Chronic primary hypoadrenalism is Addison disease: the whole cortex shuts down, so the patient makes no glucocorticoids, no aldosterone and no androgens, and has a mix of all the deficiency symptoms. Without aldosterone, sodium is low, potassium is high and blood pressure is low. Without cortisol, glucose is low and there is fatigue and weakness. The full list on the slide: weakness, fatigue, low glucose, nausea and vomiting, weight loss, psychosis, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, low sodium, high potassium, high ACTH and an inability to withstand stress. ACTH is high because the problem is primary: with the cortex failing, feedback is lost and the pituitary keeps pushing. If the failure is secondary, at the pituitary, ACTH and the adrenal cortical hormones are both low. 2 Hypoparathyroidism: causes, low calcium with high phosphate, Chvostek and Trousseau, dental root hypoplasia Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this A dental finding of hypoparathyroidism, alongside cataracts, spotty alopecia, nail fragility and basal ganglia calcification. Chvostek: tap the cheek, the face twitches. Trousseau: compress the arm, the hand spasms. Both mean low calcium. Without PTH, the kidney does the reverse of what PTH asks: it dumps calcium and keeps phosphate. So the labs show low calcium and high phosphate. Low calcium makes nerves and muscles irritable: tetany, convulsions, laryngospasm and paresthesias. Two classic exam signs come from the same irritability. Chvostek sign is a twitch of the facial muscles when the cheek is tapped. Trousseau sign is a spasm of the hand when the arm is compressed, as with a tourniquet or blood pressure cuff. Other findings are cataracts, dental root hypoplasia, spotty alopecia, nail fragility and basal ganglia calcification. 3 Cushing syndrome lab logic: cortisol read with ACTH (pituitary, ectopic, adrenal) Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Pituitary tumor making ACTH High High ACTH drives both adrenals to make cortisol Ectopic tumor making ACTH (for example, lung cancer) High High Paraneoplastic ACTH drives the adrenals Adrenal tumor making cortisol High Low Cortisol feeds back and shuts off pituitary ACTH 4 Conn syndrome (renin low) versus secondary hyperaldosteronism (renin high) Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Conn syndrome: renin low. Renal artery stenosis, CHF or a renin-secreting tumor: renin high. Aldosterone is high in both. Primary hyperaldosteronism starts in the adrenal: an adrenal adenoma, which is Conn syndrome, or adrenocortical hyperplasia. Because the aldosterone comes from the cortex and not from the renin-angiotensin system, negative feedback on the kidney shuts renin down: aldosterone high, renin low. Secondary hyperaldosteronism starts at the kidney: congestive heart failure with diminished renal perfusion, or renal artery stenosis. The kidney isn't getting the blood it needs, so it overproduces renin, and renin drives aldosterone: aldosterone high, renin high. He added a renin-secreting tumor as another way to get the secondary pattern. "The same concept repeats itself, primary versus secondary." 5 Primary hyperparathyroidism: adenoma versus hyperplasia versus carcinoma, and how they are told apart Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Both raise PTH and calcium. One enlarged gland means adenoma; several mean hyperplasia. This is a point he made carefully: adenoma and hyperplasia cannot be told apart by laboratory testing. Both are hyperfunctioning, both raise PTH and both cause hypercalcemia. The diagnosis needs anatomic evaluation: is it a single enlarged gland or several? Adenomas in all four glands are very rare, so four enlarged glands is most likely hyperplasia, while an adenoma is usually solitary. 6 Adrenal cortex zones: salt, sugar, sex Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens), from the outside in. The slide lists glucocorticoids and androgens for both inner zones; the fasciculata is mainly glucocorticoids and the reticularis mainly androgens. The memory aid from the book: it gets sweeter as you go from outside to inside, salt, sugar, sex. 7 Pseudohypoparathyroidism: end-organ resistance with high PTH Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Pseudo means false. The patient looks as if they have hypoparathyroidism, with low calcium and high phosphate, but the glands are fine: PTH is high. The problem is end-organ resistance to PTH: the target organs, such as the kidney, don't respond to the signal, so the glands keep pushing. Patients also have developmental anomalies, short stature, short metacarpals and metatarsals, and intellectual disability (the slide uses an older term). Before making the diagnosis, rule out renal failure, malabsorption and vitamin D deficiency, since those can also give low calcium with a high PTH. 8 Secondary hyperparathyroidism: renal failure, all glands, fix the cause Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Secondary hyperparathyroidism is treated at its cause (renal failure, calcium or vitamin D deficiency); surgery, if needed, is three and a half glands. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is overactivity of the parathyroids induced by conditions that cause chronic hypocalcemia. The glands respond to low calcium as they should, but the low calcium comes from disease. The most common cause is renal failure, because the failing kidney can no longer keep calcium in balance. Calcium and vitamin D deficiencies are the other causes. The glands become hyperplastic, usually all of them. The clinical features are similar to those of primary hyperparathyroidism, but less severe. When it is treated surgically, the operation is a three-and-a-half gland parathyroidectomy. But he stressed that the most important step is solving the primary issue: fix the vitamin D deficiency, and calcium and the parathyroids go back to normal. 9 Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: 21-hydroxylase versus 17-hydroxylase, treated with glucocorticoids Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank How common The most common form, several variants Less common Androgens Excess: clitoral hypertrophy, pseudohermaphroditism, oligomenorrhea, acne, hirsutism, precocious puberty Deficiency: no secondary sex characteristics in females, pseudohermaphroditism in males Sodium About a third waste sodium (aldosterone deficiency) Retained, from precursors with mineralocorticoid activity Blood pressure Low in salt wasters High Treatment Glucocorticoids Glucocorticoids 10 Addison disease: features, high ACTH, autoimmune cause Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Causes: autoimmune destruction, 60 to 70 percent, the most common; viral infection, such as herpes, CMV and AIDS; chronic infection, fungal or tuberculosis; metastatic cancer, from the lung, breast or melanoma; and systemic disease, such as amyloidosis, sarcoidosis and hemochromatosis, in which iron or amyloid deposits in the cortex and shuts it down. 11 Pheochromocytoma (rule of 10s, Zellballen) and neuroblastoma Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Pheochromocytoma (and paraganglioma) cells grow in nests or balls: Zellballen. The medulla is made of chromaffin cells, neuroendocrine cells, and a pheochromocytoma is a tumor of these neural crest chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla. It secretes catecholamines, so the patient has sweating, palpitations, paroxysmal attacks and hypertension; he added arrhythmia and a fast heart rate. Grossly, the bright golden cortex is pushed to the side by a pinkish-red medullary mass. Under the microscope the cells form nests, or balls, sitting next to each other. The German pathologist who first described them called the pattern Zellballen, which means cell balls. In children, instead of a pheochromocytoma, the medulla can give rise to neuroblastoma, a very aggressive malignant childhood tumor. About 80 percent occur under age 5. It can arise anywhere in the sympathetic nervous system, most often in the abdomen, from the adrenal medulla or the retroperitoneal sympathetic ganglia, and it metastasizes to bone, liver, lung and lymph nodes. It is hard to survive, and he called it very rare, a tumor of the pediatric age group. Under the microscope it looks primitive: whenever you hear the word "blast," it means the precursor, the immature form of a cell. Between the small primitive cells is a pink fibrillary material that resembles glial brain tissue. Also flagged in class The parathyroids are posterior to the thyroid, which is why a thyroidectomy can take them out. Expected percent of cells is about 100 minus the age. A gland at 70 to 80 percent cells in a middle-aged or older person is hypercellular and may be hyperfunctioning. Kidney stones, bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica) and neuromuscular complaints, though most patients now are found on routine labs with no symptoms. Parathyroid carcinoma: very high, symptomatic calcium, an ill-defined invasive mass, pleomorphic nuclei and necrosis. Very rare: he has probably seen one. Intraoperative PTH: a fall of more than 50 percent, not a normal value, means the gland is out. It works because PTH lasts minutes. Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH high, calcium low, phosphate high. (He said "kidney failure" while explaining it; true renal failure is a look-alike to rule out.) Read cortisol with ACTH. He said "cortisone" in places; the hormone is cortisol. Glucocorticoid lowers ACTH, which quiets the whole pathway and the androgen excess. Functional adrenal cortical adenoma = aldosterone (high sodium, low potassium, hypertension). Virilizing adrenal tumor = usually carcinoma. Neuroblastoma is a primitive, very aggressive childhood tumor (80 percent under 5); adults get olfactory neuroblastoma in the roof of the nose. You can skip Frozen section was the old way to confirm parathyroid tissue during surgery; intraoperative PTH has largely replaced it. He showed the whole steroid pathway but taught only what the 21- and 17-hydroxylase blocks do. Know those two. The rule of 10s is approximate, but it is what the slide teaches: 10 percent familial, extra-adrenal, bilateral and malignant.
